atoms.text: The replaced plank: an object's parts are swapped one by one until none of the originals remain, so continuity is asserted without a physical basis.
The preserved relic: a community maintains a sacred object through constant repair, so tradition is a maintenance schedule.
The rival reconstruction: someone collects the discarded parts and rebuilds a second version, so two claimants exist for one identity.
The ship as legal person: a vessel has rights and a name that persist through total replacement, so identity is granted by paperwork.
The crew that replaces itself: sailors retire and are replaced one at a time, so the group's identity outlives every member.
The museum's dilemma: curators must decide which of two ships is the authentic exhibit, so scholarship becomes a custody battle.
The gradual upload: a mind is transferred piece by piece into a new substrate, so the subject can never point to the moment they stopped being themselves.
The ritual of replacement: each new part is installed with ceremony, so change is made visible and deniable at once.
The original part: one component is secretly never replaced, so the whole claim of continuity rests on a hidden exception.
The child who asks: a young character points out that the ship is not the same, so an obvious observation undoes adult consensus.
The body that replaces itself: a person's cells turn over completely over years, so the paradox applies to the reader's own flesh.
The two ships in the harbor: both vessels are displayed as the original, so the public must choose which history to believe.
The identity that survives use: a tool is valued for what it has done rather than what it is made of, so function grounds continuity.
The replacement that changes behavior: each new part subtly alters how the object works, so preservation gradually becomes transformation.
The heir who refuses the relic: a descendant rejects the maintained object as a fake, so inheritance is refused on metaphysical grounds.
The paradox as a contract: two parties agree to treat the repaired object as original for practical purposes, so identity is a useful fiction.
